squeal

SKWEEL · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To squeal is to make a high, sharp cry or sound.

The toddler squealed with delight when the puppy licked her nose.

Example

Worn brake pads made the old van squeal at every red light.

The van's brakes gave off a high, piercing sound -- machines as well as people and animals can squeal.

How Strong Is It?

squeak → squeal → shriek

squeak vs. squeal

squeak vs. squeal: A squeak is small and brief, like a mouse or a floorboard -- a squeal is longer, louder, and sharper.

shriek vs. squeal

shriek vs. squeal: A shriek is even wilder than a squeal -- a piercing scream of terror, pain, or excitement.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — squeal: imitative -- the word was built to sound like the noise itself (Middle English (squelen))

Put it together: Squeal has no Latin or Greek pieces to take apart -- it's an imitative word: Middle English speakers built it to sound like the noise itself, the same way squeak and screech were built.

Use the root in a new word: squeak: One loose floorboard would squeak and give away every midnight trip to the kitchen.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Squeal covers happy, scared, and mechanical sounds alike -- children, pigs, tires, brakes. Informally, 'to squeal on someone' means to inform on them ('the getaway driver squealed to the police'), but the sound sense is the one tested here.
